Monkeypox

By: Ayanda Charlie | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Could SA manage an outbreak? As monkeypox cases grow in non-endemic countries, is South Africa prepared for its potential first human monkeypox case?

Unique Selling Point:
While Central and West African health professionals have battled the monkeypox for decades, only recent human cases in non-endemic countries are garnering attention. We're platforming African epidemiologists to share their expertise and what they make of the West's hypocrisy.

Summary:
We talk to four experts from the UK, Cameroon, and South Africa, as we answer the questions; what is monkeypox? how do we protect ourselves from it? what do we know about the latest outbreak? and is South Africa prepared to potentially have our first human case of monkeypox in history?

Further information:
To date, more than 1,000 confirmed cases of monkeypox have been reported to WHO from 29 countries that are not endemic for the disease. No monkeypox-related deaths have been reported, and while the smallpox virus is 85% effective against monkeypox, the WHO is not yet recommending mass vaccination for the virus. But, many around the world, now 'twice shy' after finding themselves in a global pandemic that blind-sided virologists all over the world, are asking themselves if this is the next global health crisis they will have to survive.

But the panic may be ill-informed as monkeypox has been endemic to Central and West African countries since the 1970s, but has received very little attention from the West even as it has afflicted thousands of Africans for decades. Although the West African clade of monkeypox virus infection sometimes leads to severe illness in some individuals, the disease is usually self-limiting. The case-fatality ratio for the West African clade has been documented to be around 1%, whereas, for the Central African clade, it may be as high as 10%. Even still, the 2022 monkeypox outbreak in non-endemic countries seems to be that of much less deadly West African Clade. So, this begs the question: why the sudden panic? and should South Africans be worried?

To answer these questions we have four experts who offer different perspectives on the current, previous, and potential future monkeypox outbreaks. Dr. Florette Treurnicht who is the head of the virology department at Wits University will walk us through what the monkeypox virus is using a visual lecture-style demonstration of the life cycle of the virus in a human host, from infection to its dormancy. The principal medical scientist at the NICD, Dr. Jacqulin Weyer, will tell us what to expect if and when the first human monkeypox case hits our shores. Cameroonian epidemiologist, Yap Boum, will offer the perspective of African health professionals who have been dealing with monkeypox for decades with limited resources and no vaccine as the West ignored their pleas for aid. Now that the virus is becoming "everyone's problem, he'll share with us what he and his colleagues hope to see change. And lastly, Professor Geoff Smith, head of the virology division at Cambridge University will elaborate on the phenomenon that is the current monkeypox outbreak in the UK, including what we're learning about the virus at this stage.

Our exploration will take us into the NHLS labs at Charlotte Maxeke Academic Hospital, where we will see the potential site of the first South African human monkeypox specimen testing. We'll hit the streets of Jo'burg to find out how much South Africans know about monkeypox, and whether or not they feel prepared for a potential outbreak. And we'll sit down with our international experts via Zoom in the Cube workspace offices, where the cosmopolitan-styled boardroom will illustrate the cross-continental spread of the virus.

Extra Budget Items:
No extra budget items.

VOX

UPSOUND
5 News Anchor: You might have heard some news about a new infection which is starting to spread in the UK.

VO: It's May 7th, 2022. In London, the British Health Security Agency confirms a case of monkeypox. In just a week, more cases trickle in.

UPSOUND
SABC News Anchor: Now, the first case of monkeypox has been identified in Scotland, bringing the number of cases in the UK to 21.


Various news reporters: Monkeypox has now been detected in 3 more countries.

The agency have identified 11 more cases in England.

Why so many people developing monkeypox around…

VO
Before the world even knows what monkeypox is, 183 cases are confirmed across the UK by the end of May. In South Africa, the penny hasn’t dropped.

Voxxie 1


Mac
Have you ever heard of monkeypox?
Young man: I haven’t.
Young woman: I don’t really know much about it. I think I just saw pictures of it, and it was just really disgusting.

VO:By mid June, over a thousand cases appear all over the world. Most of them unrelated to travel. Scientists explain: this is not a new virus. But, until now, it’s rarely left West and Central Africa and it’s never spread this wide.

UPSOUND
Piero Olliaro: But the problem is that not enough research is being done.

Yap Boum: We still don’t know exactly how the transmission has been occurring

VO: And then…

UPSOUND


Health Minister Dr. Joe Phaahla: Late yesterday, I received a report from the National Health Laboratory Service, indicating that they have confirmed, through laboratory tests, the first case of monkeypox in South Africa.

VO: A 30-year-old male in Johannesburg with no recent travel history became our first human case of monkeypox ever. With a global pandemic hardly behind us, and a new virus emerging, I went back to school for a crash course on monkeypox.Dr Florette Treurnicht is the Head of the Virology Department at WIts University.

UPSOUNDS


Mac: How worried should we be in South Africa with regards to all of this? Because It seems like there's a world panic around monkeypox.


Florette: You know, monkeypox thus far has stayed localised in West Africa. You had a few cases that were exported before I think, I would say 2021, but they were contained quite quickly. At the moment, the concern is that there were probably transmissions happening that were unnoticed.


VO: Scientists suspect that monkeypox has become better at evading the immune system so it can continue to spread and survive. So, in countries where monkeypox is new, cases unrelated to travel mean that the source is a mystery

UPSOUND


Florette: So monkeypox is a virus that is normally found in animals, and causes then this syndrome in monkeys. But sometimes it will spill over into humans. And actually the name monkeypox,is actually a bit of a misnomer, because if you look at Africa, the animals that actually carry the virus includes monkeys, squirrels, rats, and ant-eaters and sloths.




Mac: In other words any animal can actually carry it, it's just the poor monkeys the one being blamed for all this.


Florette: That's exactly what's happening at the moment. And, so, after the virus is then in humans, we get human to human transmission.

VO: Most transmissions happen through skin-to-skin contact. Then, even that dry scab will still have a live virus in it.



VO:This means that sharing clothes or touching surfaces that have been exposed to infected individuals can give you monkeypox.
Like other viruses, monkeypox can be transmitted during prolonged face to face contact but not as easily as the flu or COVID. If you’re infected, you’ll start to feel a fever coming on, followed by headaches, muscle and back pain, fatigue and even swollen lymph nodes. About 3 days in, you’ll start to notice a rash or lesions beginning to form.

UPSOUND


Florette: In 95% of cases they've got lesions in the face, inside of the palms, even on the soles of the feet, and then the genital area.


VO: While sexual contact is a common way to get it, monkeypox is not an Sexually transmitted Disease, and anyone can be infected, regardless of their sexual orientation. The World Health organisation says newborns, children and immunocompromised people may suffer worse symptoms and even die from monkeypox.

VO: Dr Jacqueline Weyer is the principal medical scientist at the National Institute for Communicable diseases.
She says that our health system can handle this outbreak. In fact, there’s a recent success story to prove it.


UPSOUND


Dr Weyer: In May 2022, we actually had an importation of a case of Lassa fever to South Africa.


VO: Lassa fever is an animal borne disease also found in parts of West Africa and poses a similar level of risk to monkeypox.
UPSOUND


Dr Weyer: So, we were able to identify the case, diagnose the case, and there were no additional cases of Lassa fever in South Africa. And we're working to make sure that we can repeat these successes.


VO: Scientists are warning that outbreaks like these will become the new normal.

UPSOUND

Dr Weyer: As we continue to put pressure on nature as our behaviour dictates. Of course, the way that we respond to it also needs to change, so that is the challenge for scientists and
that is the challenge for the healthcare systems.And experts like Oxford’s Piero Olliaro agree

Peiro: It's about human expansion; it is the invasion of natural habitats, deforestation, as we know all too well…
Link.While the rest of the world might just be finding out about monkeypox, scientists and health professionals in the central and West African regions have been dealing with this virus since the 1970s.


UPSOUND
Yap Boum: I recall was talking with one of my aunties, who was telling me that she has been seeing kids and people around her for very many years, so she was really surprised now that it's becoming a big deal.


VO: Professor Yap Boum II is a virologist for the Doctors without Borders research Arm based in Cameroon.
Boum says virologists in this region have managed to keep outbreaks relatively under control despite having limited resources, and he believes that other countries will be able to do the same.



UPSOUND
But we have to make sure that we are talking about the very same disease, because we can have the same virus which can act very differently based on the population.

VO
Research into monkeypox has been ongoing in countries like the Central African Republic and has only recently started in Europe

Professor Olliaro has been in the coalface of it


UPSOUND
Piero Olliaro: It has been disappointing that the world is waking up to monkeypox... only when it hits rich countries and it's been largely ignored before,


VO: He says more investment should be dedicated to rare disease research long before outbreaks spillover to the west. Nonetheless, this outbreak seems to be moving the needle. A clinical trial for a drug that could fight monkeypox has started in the Central African Republic.

UPSOUND


Yap:This drug has been there for some time, and there have not been enough resources.

VO: There’s also been a push to produce more monkeypox tests
But unlike we’ve seen with the response to COVID-19, Boum says a vaccine may not be a priority.

UPSOUND


Yap: Because, if, at some point, they realize that eventually there is no death, the disease stops by itself, most likely they won't push that hard to get the vaccine. because as we all know, the pharmaceutical company's aim is to make profit. That's the first thing.



VO: As numbers continue to rise across the world, the NICD expects more cases in the weeks to come, and urges all South Africans to be vigilant

We're platforming African epidemiologists to share their expertise and what they make of the West's hypocrisy.
metadata.Summary: We talk to four experts from the UK, Cameroon, and South Africa, as we answer the questions; what is monkeypox? how do we protect ourselves from it? what do we know about the latest outbreak? and is South Africa prepared to potentially have our first human case of monkeypox in history?
metadata.Further information: To date, more than 1,000 confirmed cases of monkeypox have been reported to WHO from 29 countries that are not endemic for the disease. No monkeypox-related deaths have been reported, and while the smallpox virus is 85% effective against monkeypox, the WHO is not yet recommending mass vaccination for the virus. But, many around the world, now 'twice shy' after finding themselves in a global pandemic that blind-sided virologists all over the world, are asking themselves if this is the next global health crisis they will have to survive. But the panic may be ill-informed as monkeypox has been endemic to Central and West African countries since the 1970s, but has received very little attention from the West even as it has afflicted thousands of Africans for decades. Although the West African clade of monkeypox virus infection sometimes leads to severe illness in some individuals, the disease is usually self-limiting. The case-fatality ratio for the West African clade has been documented to be around 1%, whereas, for the Central African clade, it may be as high as 10%. Even still, the 2022 monkeypox outbreak in non-endemic countries seems to be that of much less deadly West African Clade. So, this begs the question: why the sudden panic? and should South Africans be worried? To answer these questions we have four experts who offer different perspectives on the current, previous, and potential future monkeypox outbreaks. Dr. Florette Treurnicht who is the head of the virology department at Wits University will walk us through what the monkeypox virus is using a visual lecture-style demonstration of the life cycle of the virus in a human host, from infection to its dormancy. The principal medical scientist at the NICD, Dr. Jacqulin Weyer, will tell us what to expect if and when the first human monkeypox case hits our shores. Cameroonian epidemiologist, Yap Boum, will offer the perspective of African health professionals who have been dealing with monkeypox for decades with limited resources and no vaccine as the West ignored their pleas for aid. Now that the virus is becoming "everyone's problem, he'll share with us what he and his colleagues hope to see change. And lastly, Professor Geoff Smith, head of the virology division at Cambridge University will elaborate on the phenomenon that is the current monkeypox outbreak in the UK, including what we're learning about the virus at this stage. Our exploration will take us into the NHLS labs at Charlotte Maxeke Academic Hospital, where we will see the potential site of the first South African human monkeypox specimen testing. We'll hit the streets of Jo'burg to find out how much South Africans know about monkeypox, and whether or not they feel prepared for a potential outbreak. And we'll sit down with our international experts via Zoom in the Cube workspace offices, where the cosmopolitan-styled boardroom will illustrate the cross-continental spread of the virus.
